transcript.text:
Try these checks first:

1. Check power
• Interior light on? Plug firmly in?
• Check breaker/GFCI outlet.
• If it was just plugged in or moved, allow 4–6 hours to cool.

2. Check temperature settings
• Set fridge to about 3–4°C / 37–40°F and freezer to -18°C / 0°F.
• Avoid setting it to the warmest setting accidentally.

3. Make sure air can circulate
• Don’t pack food tightly against vents, especially at the back.
• Ensure doors fully close; inspect the gasket for gaps, dirt, or torn rubber.
• A simple test: close the door on a piece of paper—there should be noticeable resistance when pulling it out.

4. Clean the condenser area
• Unplug the fridge.
• Vacuum dust from the coils/vent area (usually underneath or behind the unit), then plug it back in.
• Leave clearance around the refrigerator for ventilation.

5. Listen/look for clues
• Freezer cold but fridge warm: likely blocked air vent, failed evaporator fan, iced-over evaporator, or damper issue. Check for heavy frost on the freezer’s back panel.
• Both fridge and freezer warm: possible power issue, compressor/start relay failure, condenser fan issue, or sealed-system/refrigerant problem.
• Compressor runs constantly but little cooling: usually needs professional service.

### Food safety
If the fridge is above 4°C / 40°F for more than 2 hours (or 1 hour if the room is very hot), discard perishable foods such as meat, dairy, cooked leftovers, and eggs. Keep the doors closed as much as possible.

### Call for repair soon if
• The fridge is warm but running continuously
• You hear clicking every few minutes
• There is a burning smell, hot plug, or tripped breaker
• There is heavy frost buildup
• Cleaning and settings don’t improve cooling after 12–24 hours

Tell me: is the freezer still cold, are the lights on, and do you hear the fridge running?
freezer still cold, light on, motor running a lot. no burning smell or tripping

Since the freezer is cold, the compressor is running, and power is fine, this is most often an airflow problem from freezer to refrigerator rather than a major compressor failure.

Try this:

1. Check refrigerator air vents
• Look for vents at the back/top of the fridge compartment.
• Move food away from them; don’t block them with containers or bags.
• Make sure the fridge temperature control isn’t set to “warm” or “off.”

2. Check for frost in the freezer
• Look at the rear inside wall of the freezer.
• If it has a thick layer of frost/ice, the evaporator may be iced over. That blocks cold air from reaching the fridge.

3. Check the freezer fan
• Open the freezer door and find/hold down the door switch (the small button that turns the light off when the door closes).
• You should hear a fan running behind the freezer’s rear panel.
• No fan sound may mean a failed evaporator fan or switch.

4. Check the air damper
• Many units have a vent/damper where cold freezer air enters the fridge, often near the top rear.
• It may be stuck shut or blocked by ice.

### If there is heavy frost
A full manual defrost can temporarily restore it:

• Move food to a cooler if possible.
• Unplug the refrigerator.
• Leave both doors open for at least 12–24 hours with towels around it.
• Do not chip ice with a knife or sharp tool.
• Plug it back in and allow several hours to cool.

If it works after defrosting but becomes warm again within days or weeks, the likely cause is a failed defrost heater, defrost sensor/thermostat, control board, or fan, and it needs repair.

Also vacuum the dust around the lower/back condenser area if accessible, since a dirty condenser can make it run excessively—though with a cold freezer and warm fridge, frost/airflow is still more likely.

Keep perishable fridge food below 4°C / 40°F; if it has been warmer than that for over about 2 hours, discard risky items such as meat, dairy, leftovers, and cooked foods.

moved food from the back, no difference. hardly any cold air from the slots. thick white frost on the back wall of the freezer, more than ive ever seen. faint scraping/ticking from the freezer sometimes. no idea about the damper

That strongly points to an iced-over evaporator/defrost-system problem.

The thick frost on the freezer’s back wall is blocking the evaporator coils and the airflow passages to the fridge. The faint scraping/ticking is likely the freezer evaporator fan hitting ice. That explains why the freezer remains cold while little cold air reaches the refrigerator section.

### What to do now
1. Move perishables to a cooler or another fridge/freezer.
2. Unplug the refrigerator.
3. Leave both doors open for 24 hours; with unusually heavy ice, 36–48 hours is safer.
4. Put towels around the base for meltwater.
5. Do not chip ice with a knife or screwdriver—it can puncture refrigerant lines.
6. Once fully thawed and dry, plug it back in. It may take several hours to return to normal temperature.

You do not need to find the damper before doing this—the frost needs to be cleared first.

### What happens next
• If the fridge cools normally after defrosting but frost returns within days or a few weeks, a part of the automatic defrost system is likely faulty: commonly the defrost heater, temperature sensor/thermostat, control board/timer, or possibly the evaporator fan.
• If the fan still scrapes or does not run once everything is fully thawed, it likely needs service/replacement.
• If it does not start sending cold air to the refrigerator after a complete defrost, the damper or fan should be checked by a technician.

Avoid leaving it running in its current frosted state—it will keep running hard without cooling the fridge properly.
